Chapter overview

Early resistance against Company rule moved from Palayakkarar confederacies and restoration struggles to the broad Marudhu appeal, Kongu guerrilla warfare and the sepoy uprising at Vellore.

Palayakkarar systemRegional confederaciesSivaganga & PanchalankurichiKongu resistanceVellore 1806
Scope, Chronology and Nature of Early Resistance

Early anti-Company resistance in Tamil Nadu extended from Puli Thevar’s struggle in 1755 to the Vellore military uprising of 1806 and differed in purpose and organisation from the later national movement.

Scope

Early resistance in Tamil Nadu developed when the East India Company expanded its territorial, military and revenue authority after the Carnatic Wars.

The main phase covered in this chapter extends from:

  • Puli Thevar’s resistance beginning in 1755
  • To the Vellore Revolt of 1806

The major centres were located in:

  • Tirunelveli
  • Thoothukudi
  • Sivaganga
  • Dindigul
  • Kongu region
  • Vellore
Main Forms of Resistance

The early agitations included:

  • Refusal to pay Company-controlled revenue
  • Defence of Palayakkarar autonomy
  • Formation of military confederacies
  • Fort-based warfare
  • Guerrilla attacks
  • Alliances with Mysore, Travancore and the French
  • Public proclamations against Company rule
  • Military uprising by Indian sepoys
Nature of the Resistance

These struggles differed from the later national movement.

Early resistance generally aimed to:

  • Protect inherited territories
  • Restore displaced rulers
  • Preserve regional political authority
  • Resist Company revenue collection
  • Reverse British territorial expansion

They did not initially operate through an all-India nationalist organisation. However, the Marudhu proclamation expanded the appeal beyond one kingdom or Palayam by calling upon different groups to unite against British authority.

Sources

Important sources include:

  • East India Company correspondence
  • Revenue records
  • Military reports
  • Trial proceedings
  • Treaties
  • Proclamations
  • Local ballads
  • Oral traditions
  • Memorial records

Colonial records often described the leaders as rebels or disturbers of peace. Local traditions remembered them as defenders of political freedom. Both forms of evidence must be assessed carefully.

Palayakkarar System and Company Revenue Expansion

The Palayakkarar system combined territorial administration, revenue collection and military service; Company attempts to take over revenue sovereignty transformed fiscal disputes into political conflict.

Meaning of Palayam

The word Palayam could refer to:

  • A domain
  • A military camp
  • A small territorial kingdom

The British referred to a Palayakkarar as a Poligar.

Origin of the System

A form of the Palayakkarar system existed in the Kakatiya kingdom of Warangal.

In Tamil Nadu, the system was organised under:

  • Viswanatha Nayaka
  • Ariyanatha Mudaliar

Viswanatha Nayaka became the ruler of Madurai in 1529.

Tradition refers to 72 Palayams under the Madurai Nayak system.

Duties of the Palayakkarars

They were authorised to:

  • Collect revenue
  • Administer their territories
  • Maintain armed forces
  • Settle disputes
  • Maintain law and order
  • Perform military service for the superior ruler

Their policing duties were known as:

  • Padikaval
  • Arasu Kaval
Eastern and Western Palayams

Important eastern Palayams included:

  • Sattur
  • Nagalapuram
  • Ettayapuram
  • Panchalankurichi

Important western Palayams included:

  • Uthumalai
  • Thalavankottai
  • Naduvakurichi
  • Singampatti
  • Seithur

The western Palayams formed the main support base of Puli Thevar.

Revenue Authority of the Company

The Nawab of Arcot borrowed heavily from the East India Company during the Carnatic Wars.

As the Nawab’s debts increased:

  • The Company acquired authority to collect revenue from the southern Palayams.
  • Company collectors demanded tribute or kist.
  • Palayakkarars claimed hereditary rights over their territories.
  • Many refused to recognise Company revenue authority.
  • The Company classified resisting chiefs as rebels.

The conflict was therefore not merely over unpaid tax. It concerned the transfer of political and revenue sovereignty from regional authorities to a foreign commercial company.

Puli Thevar: Confederacy and Battle of Kalakadu

Puli Thevar organised the western Palayakkarars and defeated Mahfuz Khan’s forces at Kalakadu, demonstrating the importance of regional alliances against Company expansion.

Puli Thevar

Puli Thevar was the Palayakkarar of:

  • Nerkattumseval
  • Tirunelveli region

His main resistance lasted from:

  • 1755 to 1767

The Tamil Nadu textbook identifies his struggle as the first resistance in Tamil Nadu to the East India Company’s policy of territorial expansion.

Avoid converting this into an unqualified claim that he was the first freedom fighter of the whole of India.

Colonel Heron’s Expedition

In March 1755:

  • Mahfuz Khan, brother of the Nawab of Arcot, proceeded to Tirunelveli.
  • Company forces accompanied him.
  • Colonel Heron commanded the Company contingent.
  • Madurai fell to their forces.
  • Heron was then directed against Puli Thevar.

Heron abandoned the attack because of:

  • Lack of heavy cannon
  • Inadequate supplies
  • Difficulty in paying soldiers

He withdrew to Madurai and was later recalled and dismissed.

Puli Thevar’s Confederacy

Puli Thevar formed an alliance of western Palayakkarars.

He maintained contact with three Pathan officers who had served as agents of Chanda Sahib:

  • Mianah
  • Mudimiah
  • Nabikhan Kattak

Most Maravar Palayams supported Puli Thevar.

Important exceptions included:

  • Sivagiri
  • Ettayapuram
  • Panchalankurichi

The Company secured the support of:

  • Ramanathapuram
  • Pudukkottai

Puli Thevar also attempted to obtain assistance from:

  • Hyder Ali
  • The French

Hyder Ali could not assist him because he was engaged in conflict with the Marathas.

Battle of Kalakadu

Mahfuz Khan advanced with:

  • Company sepoys
  • Additional troops sent by the Nawab
  • Cavalry
  • Infantry from the Carnatic

About 2,000 Travancore soldiers joined Puli Thevar’s forces.

At the Battle of Kalakadu:

  • Mahfuz Khan’s forces were defeated.
  • The victory strengthened the western Palayakkarar resistance.
  • It demonstrated Puli Thevar’s ability to build regional alliances.
Puli Thevar, Yusuf Khan and Ondiveeran

Yusuf Khan’s artillery campaign weakened Puli Thevar’s confederacy, while Ondiveeran remains associated with Puli Thevar’s army and oral traditions of battlefield courage.

Yusuf Khan

Yusuf Khan was also known as:

  • Khan Sahib
  • Marudhanayagam before his conversion to Islam

The Company sent him to suppress the Palayakkarar resistance.

Between 1756 and 1763:

  • Puli Thevar and the western Palayakkarars repeatedly resisted the authority of the Nawab and Company.
  • Yusuf Khan waited for heavy artillery before attacking Nerkattumseval.
  • The required cannon and ammunition arrived in September 1760.
Loss of Puli Thevar’s Forts

Yusuf Khan attacked Nerkattumseval for about two months.

On 16 May 1761, three major forts came under his control:

  • Nerkattumseval
  • Vasudevanallur
  • Panayur
Collapse of the Confederacy

The British capture of Pondicherry weakened the possibility of French support.

Several former allies changed sides:

  • Travancore
  • Seithur
  • Uthumalai
  • Surandai

Yusuf Khan later negotiated with the Palayakkarars without informing the Company administration.

He was:

  • Accused of treachery
  • Executed in 1764
Return and Final Defeat of Puli Thevar

After Yusuf Khan’s death:

  • Puli Thevar returned from exile.
  • He recovered Nerkattumseval in 1764.
  • Captain Campbell defeated him in 1767.
  • Puli Thevar escaped and died in exile.
Ondiveeran

Ondiveeran commanded one of Puli Thevar’s army units.

He is remembered for:

  • Entering enemy positions
  • Inflicting damage on Company forces
  • Continuing to fight despite severe injury

The story of the loss of his hand is preserved mainly through oral tradition and should be identified as such.

Ondiveeran must be associated with Puli Thevar, not with Kattabomman.

Velu Nachiyar and the Recovery of Sivaganga

After the 1772 attack on Kalaiyar Kovil, Velu Nachiyar used alliances with Gopala Nayak, Hyder Ali and the Marudhu Brothers to recover Sivaganga in 1780.

Early Life

Velu Nachiyar was born in 1730 into the royal family of Ramanathapuram.

Her father was:

  • Sellamuthu Sethupathi

She received training in:

  • Valari
  • Stick fighting
  • Weapon use
  • Horse riding
  • Archery

The textbook also associates her with knowledge of:

  • Tamil
  • English
  • French
  • Urdu

She married:

  • Muthu Vaduganatha Thevar, ruler of Sivaganga

Their daughter was:

  • Vellachi Nachiyar
Attack on Kalaiyar Kovil

In 1772:

  • The Nawab of Arcot and Company troops attacked Kalaiyar Kovil.
  • Lieutenant Colonel Bon Jour commanded the attacking force.
  • Muthu Vaduganatha Thevar was killed.
  • Velu Nachiyar escaped with her daughter.

She received protection at Virupachi from:

  • Gopala Nayak

She remained outside Sivaganga for approximately eight years.

Alliances

Velu Nachiyar organised an army and secured support from:

  • Gopala Nayak
  • Hyder Ali
  • Marudhu Brothers

Her military chief Thandavarayanar sought assistance from Hyder Ali.

The request referred to:

  • 5,000 infantry
  • 5,000 cavalry

Hyder Ali directed his commandant at Dindigul to assist her.

Recovery of Sivaganga

Velu Nachiyar:

  • Gathered intelligence about enemy positions
  • Reorganised her forces
  • Recovered Sivaganga
  • Returned to rule in 1780

The Marudhu Brothers became central figures in the restored administration:

  • Periya Marudhu served as military commander.
  • Chinna Marudhu exercised ministerial authority.
Kuyili

Kuyili is remembered as:

  • A close associate of Velu Nachiyar
  • Leader of a women’s military unit
  • A participant in the attack on the enemy ammunition store

The account of her self-sacrificial attack is strongly preserved in Tamil commemorative tradition. It should be presented with appropriate source caution rather than as a fully documented battlefield report.

This topic covers the military recovery of Sivaganga. The wider significance of Velu Nachiyar, Kuyili and women’s military participation belongs in Chapter 19.

Gopala Nayak and the Dindigul League

Gopala Nayak made Virupachi a refuge and resistance centre and organised the Dindigul League, linking Sivaganga, Kongu and the later South Indian confederacy.

Gopala Nayak was the Palayakkarar of:

  • Virupachi near Dindigul
Dindigul League

Gopala Nayak organised the Dindigul League with leaders including:

  • Lakshmi Nayak of Manaparai
  • Poojai Nayak of Devadanapatti

The league sought to coordinate resistance against British expansion.

Relationship with Mysore
  • Gopala Nayak drew encouragement from Tipu Sultan.
  • Tipu reportedly sent representatives to maintain contact.
  • Virupachi became a refuge and organising centre for anti-Company leaders.
Support to Velu Nachiyar

Gopala Nayak:

  • Gave protection to Velu Nachiyar and her daughter.
  • Assisted in rebuilding her military forces.
  • Helped her obtain support from Hyder Ali.
  • Participated in the recovery of Sivaganga.
Wider Resistance

He later:

  • Organised opposition in the Coimbatore region
  • Worked with Oomathurai
  • Fought in the Anaimalai hills
  • Received support from local peasants

In April 1800, Virupachi became a meeting place for leaders planning a wider uprising.

Gopala Nayak was defeated by British forces in 1801.

He forms an important link between:

  • Velu Nachiyar’s restoration
  • Kongu resistance
  • Oomathurai
  • Marudhu-led South Indian Confederacy
Kattabomman and the Jackson Confrontation

Kattabomman’s 1798 confrontation with Collector Jackson exposed Company coercion, but the inquiry that cleared him did not resolve the larger struggle over political and revenue authority.

Veerapandiya Kattabomman

Veerapandiya Kattabomman became the Palayakkarar of:

  • Panchalankurichi

He assumed office in 1790 after the death of his father:

  • Jagavira Pandya Kattabomman

Panchalankurichi is written as Panchalamkurichi in some textbook editions.

Cause of the Conflict

Under an arrangement made by the Nawab of Arcot:

  • The Company secured authority to collect revenue from the Palayams.
  • Company collectors attempted to enforce payments directly.
  • The collectors often treated Palayakkarars with humiliation.
  • Kattabomman resisted Company interference and coercive revenue collection.

His recorded revenue arrears in 1798 were:

  • 3,310 pagodas
Collector Jackson’s Summons

Collector Colin Jackson ordered Kattabomman to meet him at Ramanathapuram.

Kattabomman attempted to meet him at:

  • Courtallam
  • Srivilliputhur

Jackson refused to grant him an audience at these places.

The meeting finally occurred at Ramanathapuram on:

  • 19 September 1798

Kattabomman was reportedly forced to stand for several hours before Jackson.

Clash at Ramanathapuram

Sensing danger, Kattabomman attempted to leave with his minister:

  • Sivasubramanianar

Oomathurai entered with armed supporters and assisted Kattabomman’s escape.

During the clash:

  • Lieutenant Clarke was killed.
  • Sivasubramanianar was captured.
Inquiry by the Madras Council

Kattabomman complained to the Madras Council about Jackson’s conduct.

A committee consisting of:

  • William Brown
  • William Oram
  • John Casamajor

examined the incident.

On 15 December 1798:

  • Kattabomman appeared before the committee.
  • The committee found him not guilty.
  • Jackson was dismissed.
  • S. R. Lushington became the new collector.

Kattabomman paid most of the arrears, leaving a reported balance of:

  • 1,080 pagodas

The Jackson episode alone did not end the conflict because the deeper issue of Company political authority remained unresolved.

Siege of Panchalankurichi and Execution of Kattabomman

Major Bannerman captured Panchalankurichi in 1799; Kattabomman was captured with allied Indian assistance and executed at Kayathar on 16 October.

Relationship with the Confederacy

The Marudhu Brothers were organising a wider South Indian confederacy.

Its associates included:

  • Gopala Nayak of Dindigul
  • Yadul Nayak of Anaimalai
  • Other neighbouring Palayakkarars

Kattabomman showed interest in the confederacy.

Collector Lushington attempted to prevent direct contact between:

  • Kattabomman
  • Marudhu Brothers

Kattabomman also attempted to influence Sivagiri, which remained aligned with the Company.

The Company interpreted his movement towards Sivagiri as a direct challenge.

Company Expedition

In May 1799:

  • Governor-General Lord Wellesley ordered military action.
  • Forces advanced from Tiruchirappalli, Thanjavur and Madurai.
  • Major Bannerman commanded the operation.
  • Travancore forces supported the Company.

An ultimatum was issued on:

  • 1 September 1799

Major Bannerman reached Panchalankurichi and began the main operation on:

  • 5 September 1799
Siege

Company forces:

  • Cut communication routes
  • Surrounded the fort
  • Demanded Kattabomman’s surrender

Bannerman sent Ramalinganar to deliver the demand.

Kattabomman refused to surrender.

Ramalinganar gathered information about the fort, which assisted Company planning.

Escape and Capture

After the fall of the fort:

  • Kattabomman escaped towards Pudukkottai.
  • A reward was announced for his capture.
  • The rulers of Ettayapuram and Pudukkottai assisted the Company.
  • Kattabomman was captured.

His minister Sivasubramanianar was:

  • Captured at Kallarpatti
  • Executed at Nagalapuram on 13 September 1799
Execution of Kattabomman

Bannerman conducted a trial before assembled Palayakkarars.

Kattabomman was executed at:

  • Kayathar
  • 16 October 1799

Tamil folk ballads and public memory preserved his resistance after his death.

Oomathurai, Sevathaiah and the Rebuilt Panchalankurichi Fort

Oomathurai and Sevathaiah escaped prison, rebuilt Panchalankurichi and joined the Marudhu Brothers, directly connecting Kattabomman’s conflict with the wider rebellion of 1800–1801.

Kattabomman’s Brothers

Kattabomman’s brothers included:

  • Oomathurai, also called Duraisingam
  • Sevathaiah, also called Dalavai Kumarasami in some traditions

Oomathurai had already assisted Kattabomman during the confrontation at Ramanathapuram.

Escape from Palayamkottai

In February 1801:

  • Oomathurai and Sevathaiah escaped from Palayamkottai prison.
  • They travelled to Kamudhi.
  • Chinna Marudhu took them to Siruvayal, the Sivaganga capital.
Reconstruction of Panchalankurichi
  • The fort at Panchalankurichi was rebuilt rapidly.
  • Oomathurai resumed armed resistance.
  • Local supporters joined the revived stronghold.

British troops under:

  • Colin Macaulay

recaptured the fort in April 1801.

Protection by the Marudhu Brothers

Oomathurai and Sevathaiah sought protection in Sivaganga.

The Company demanded their surrender.

The Marudhu Brothers refused to hand them over.

This refusal became an immediate cause for the Company’s military invasion of Sivaganga.

Capture and Execution

After the defeat of the South Indian Rebellion:

  • Oomathurai and Sevathaiah were captured.
  • They were executed at Panchalankurichi.
  • Date — 16 November 1801

Oomathurai connects the resistance of Kattabomman directly with the Marudhu-led rebellion of 1800–1801.

Marudhu Brothers and the South Indian Confederacy

The Marudhu Brothers attempted to coordinate leaders across Sivaganga, Dindigul, Kongu, Malabar and Mysore in a regional anti-Company confederacy.

Marudhu Brothers

The brothers were:

  • Periya Marudhu or Vella Marudhu — 1748–1801
  • Chinna Marudhu — 1753–1801

They initially served as commanders under:

  • Muthu Vaduganatha Thevar of Sivaganga

After his death:

  • They accompanied Velu Nachiyar.
  • They helped restore her to the Sivaganga throne.
  • They later became the principal administrative and military authorities of Sivaganga.
Expansion of Resistance

After Kattabomman’s execution:

  • The Marudhu Brothers worked with Oomathurai.
  • They attacked Company forces and the Nawab’s resources.
  • They attempted to transform scattered resistance into a regional alliance.
South Indian Confederacy

Important members and associates included:

  • Marudhu Pandiyars of Sivaganga
  • Gopala Nayak of Dindigul
  • Kerala Varma of Malabar
  • Krishnappa Nayak of Mysore
  • Dhoondaji of Mysore
  • Palayakkarars from the Kongu region

In April 1800:

  • Representatives met at Virupachi.
  • They decided to organise a coordinated uprising against the Company.
Spread of the Rebellion

The uprising began in the Coimbatore region in June 1800 and spread towards:

  • Ramanathapuram
  • Madurai
  • Dindigul
  • Sivaganga

The Company suppressed resistance in:

  • Coimbatore
  • Sathyamangalam
  • Dharapuram

Captured Palayakkarars were executed.

Terminology

The uprising is known as:

  • South Indian Rebellion
  • Second Palayakkarar War in British records

It was broader than Kattabomman’s 1799 conflict because it attempted to unite leaders across several political regions.

Tiruchirappalli or Jambudweepa Proclamation of 1801

The June 1801 proclamation appealed across caste, creed, religion and region, turning a military confederacy into a broader public call against Company domination.

Issuance

The Marudhu Brothers issued a proclamation in June 1801.

It is commonly known as:

  • Tiruchirappalli Proclamation
  • Jambudweepa Proclamation

The proclamation was publicly displayed on:

  • The walls of the Nawab’s palace in Tiruchirappalli Fort
  • The walls of the Srirangam temple

The Jambudweepa Proclamation is commemorated on:

  • 16 June
Central Message

The proclamation:

  • Condemned British domination
  • Criticised the loss of Indian political authority
  • Called upon people to oppose Company rule
  • Urged unity across region
  • Urged unity across caste
  • Urged unity across creed and religion
  • Attempted to transform regional resistance into a broader public struggle
Military Mobilisation

Chinna Marudhu reportedly gathered a force of nearly:

  • 20,000 men

The Company brought reinforcements from:

  • Bengal
  • Ceylon
  • Malaya

Several rulers supported the British, including those of:

  • Pudukkottai
  • Ettayapuram
  • Thanjavur

British diplomacy and political divisions weakened the confederacy.

Historical Importance

The proclamation was one of the earliest broad anti-Company calls issued in southern India.

It is reasonable to describe it as:

  • An early public call for united anti-colonial resistance
  • A significant political document of the South Indian Rebellion

Avoid stating without qualification that it was universally accepted as India’s first declaration of independence.

Fall of Sivaganga, Penang Deportation and Carnatic Treaty

The fall of Sivaganga, execution and deportation of rebels, and Carnatic Treaty of 1801 ended most autonomous Palayakkarar military authority and expanded direct Company rule.

Company Offensive

In 1801, Company forces attacked resistance centres in:

  • Thanjavur
  • Tiruchirappalli
  • Ramanathapuram
  • Madurai
  • Sivaganga

The rebels withdrew towards strongholds such as:

  • Piranmalai
  • Kalaiyar Kovil

The Company possessed:

  • Superior artillery
  • Larger reinforcements
  • Better logistical support
  • Assistance from allied Indian rulers
Fall of Sivaganga
  • Sivaganga was defeated and annexed in 1801.
  • The Marudhu Brothers were captured.
  • They were executed at Tiruppattur on 24 October 1801.

Oomathurai and Sevathaiah were:

  • Captured
  • Executed at Panchalankurichi on 16 November 1801
Penang Deportation

Seventy-three rebels were transported to:

  • Penang
  • Malaya

Transportation removed leaders and supporters from their regional networks and served as a severe colonial punishment.

Carnatic Treaty of 1801

The Carnatic Treaty was concluded on:

  • 31 July 1801

Its broader consequences included:

  • Expansion of direct Company control
  • Transfer of administrative authority from the Nawab of Arcot
  • End of the Palayakkarar political system
  • Demolition of forts
  • Disbanding of local armies
  • Removal of autonomous military chiefs

Districts transferred to Company administration included:

  • North Arcot
  • South Arcot
  • Tiruchirappalli
  • Madurai
  • Tirunelveli
Significance

The suppression of the rebellion ended the ability of most Palayakkarars to function as autonomous military rulers.

The Company no longer acted only as a revenue contractor. It emerged as the direct territorial authority over much of Tamil Nadu.

Dheeran Chinnamalai and Kongu Resistance

Dheeran Chinnamalai continued armed resistance in Kongu after Tipu Sultan’s death, using Odanilai, local support and mobile guerrilla methods until his execution in 1805.

Early Life

Dheeran Chinnamalai was born in 1756.

His original name was:

  • Theerthagiri

He belonged to the Mandradiar family associated with:

  • Palayakottai
  • Kongu region

He was trained in:

  • Silambam
  • Archery
  • Horse riding
  • Warfare
Origin of the Name Chinnamalai

According to the textbook account:

  • Tax from Kongu was being carried to Mysore by Tipu Sultan’s Diwan, Mohammed Ali.
  • Theerthagiri intercepted the revenue.
  • A conflict later took place near the Noyyal riverbed.
  • His identification with the region between Sivamalai and Chennimalai gave rise to the name Chinnamalai.
Alliance with Mysore

Dheeran Chinnamalai:

  • Received military training associated with the French
  • Mobilised Kongu youth
  • Fought alongside Tipu Sultan against the British

After Tipu Sultan’s death in 1799, he continued the struggle independently.

Odanilai

Dheeran Chinnamalai established a fort at:

  • Odanilai

He used:

  • Guerrilla attacks
  • Local terrain
  • Mobile military tactics
  • Support from Kongu communities

He repeatedly avoided Company capture.

Capture and Execution

The Company eventually captured:

  • Dheeran Chinnamalai
  • His brothers

They were imprisoned at Sankagiri.

They refused to accept British rule and were executed at:

  • Sankagiri Fort
  • 31 July 1805

Dheeran Chinnamalai represents the continuation of armed resistance in the Kongu region after the defeat of the major southern Palayakkarar confederacy.

Vellore Revolt: Background and Causes

The Vellore Revolt arose from military discrimination, economic hardship, political dispossession, religious anxiety and the presence of Tipu Sultan’s family inside the fort.

Political Background

Before 1806, the Company had:

  • Acquired Salem and Dindigul after conflict with Mysore
  • Annexed Coimbatore after Tipu Sultan’s defeat in 1799
  • Reduced the Thanjavur ruler’s sovereignty
  • Defeated Kattabomman
  • Suppressed the Marudhu Brothers
  • Imposed the Carnatic Treaty of 1801

Members of Tipu Sultan’s family were confined inside:

  • Vellore Fort
Economic Grievances of Sepoys

Indian soldiers faced:

  • Low pay
  • Limited chances of promotion
  • Racial discrimination
  • Disrespect from European officers

Many sepoys came from peasant families affected by:

  • Changes in land-revenue systems
  • Economic distress
  • Famine conditions in 1805
Social and Religious Grievances

The Commander-in-Chief:

  • Sir John Cradock

introduced new military regulations.

Indian soldiers in uniform were ordered:

  • Not to wear caste marks
  • Not to wear earrings
  • To shave their chins
  • To maintain regulated moustaches
  • To wear a new form of turban

The turban included a leather cockade made from animal skin.

Both Hindu and Muslim sepoys feared:

  • Interference with religious identity
  • Loss of customary practices
  • Possible forced conversion

Sepoys had already shown opposition by refusing to wear the new turban, but Company officials failed to address their grievances.

Wider Cause

The dress regulations were the immediate trigger, not the only cause.

The revolt developed from the combination of:

  • Military discrimination
  • Economic hardship
  • Religious anxiety
  • Political dispossession
  • Presence of Tipu Sultan’s family
  • Resentment following British conquest of South India
Vellore Revolt: Outbreak, Suppression and Consequences

On 10 July 1806, sepoys seized Vellore Fort and proclaimed Fateh Hyder before Colonel Gillespie suppressed the revolt; the uprising became an important precursor to 1857.

Outbreak

The revolt began in the early hours of:

  • 10 July 1806

Indian sepoys from units including the:

  • 1st Regiment
  • 23rd Regiment

rose against the European garrison.

Among the officers killed were:

  • Colonel Fancourt
  • Colonel McKerras
  • Major Armstrong
  • Several other European officers
Proclamation of Fateh Hyder

The rebels:

  • Proclaimed Fateh Hyder as ruler
  • Identified him as Tipu Sultan’s eldest son
  • Raised the tiger flag associated with the Mysore Sultans

The revolt therefore combined sepoy grievances with the possibility of restoring Mysore authority.

Suppression by Gillespie

Major Cootes, who was outside the fort, informed:

  • Colonel Robert Gillespie at Arcot

Gillespie reached Vellore with cavalry commanded by Captain Young at approximately:

  • 9 a.m.

The uprising was suppressed with extreme violence.

The textbook records an eyewitness estimate that:

  • About 800 soldiers were found dead inside the fort
  • About 600 were confined at Vellore and Tiruchirappalli pending inquiry

These figures should be identified as reported contemporary estimates.

Punishments

After the revolt:

  • Six convicted rebels were blown from guns.
  • Five were shot.
  • Eight were hanged.
  • Other soldiers received imprisonment or transportation.

Tipu Sultan’s sons were transferred to:

  • Calcutta

Gillespie received:

  • Prize money
  • Promotion
  • A reward of 7,000 pagodas
Administrative Consequences

Officials held responsible included:

  • Sir John Cradock
  • Adjutant-General Agnew
  • Governor William Bentinck

They were removed or recalled.

The controversial military regulations were withdrawn.

Indian Organisers

The textbook identifies organisers including:

  • Subedar Sheik Adam
  • Subedar Sheik Hamid
  • Jamadar Sheik Hussain
  • Jamadar Sheik Kasim
  • Other Indian non-commissioned officers
Spread and Echoes

The unrest had echoes in military centres including:

  • Walajabad
  • Bellary
  • Hyderabad
  • Bengaluru
  • Nandidurg
  • Sankaridurg
Historical Assessment

The Vellore Revolt anticipated several features later visible in 1857:

  • Sepoy rebellion
  • Religious fears
  • Resistance to military regulations
  • Connection with a displaced Indian dynasty
  • Attempt to restore an Indian ruler

However, unlike 1857:

  • It received no immediate large-scale civilian support.
  • It remained geographically limited.
  • It was suppressed within a few hours.
  • No wider civil rebellion followed it.

It should be described as a major precursor to 1857, not casually equated with the entire Revolt of 1857.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The final topic consolidates chronology, leader–place, alliance and event distinctions, together with the source cautions most useful for TNPSC elimination questions.

Essential Chronology
  • 1529 — Viswanatha Nayaka organised the Palayakkarar system in the Madurai kingdom
  • 1755 — Beginning of Puli Thevar’s principal resistance
  • 1755 — Colonel Heron’s expedition
  • 1761 — Puli Thevar’s three major forts captured by Yusuf Khan
  • 1764 — Yusuf Khan executed; Puli Thevar recovered Nerkattumseval
  • 1767 — Puli Thevar defeated by Captain Campbell
  • 1772 — Muthu Vaduganatha Thevar killed at Kalaiyar Kovil
  • 1780 — Velu Nachiyar recovered Sivaganga
  • 1790 — Kattabomman became Palayakkarar of Panchalankurichi
  • 19 September 1798 — Kattabomman met Collector Jackson
  • 15 December 1798 — Kattabomman appeared before the Madras Council committee
  • 5 September 1799 — Major Company attack on Panchalankurichi
  • 13 September 1799 — Sivasubramanianar executed
  • 16 October 1799 — Kattabomman executed at Kayathar
  • 1800–1801 — South Indian Rebellion
  • April 1800 — Confederacy meeting at Virupachi
  • February 1801 — Oomathurai and Sevathaiah escaped from prison
  • June 1801 — Tiruchirappalli or Jambudweepa Proclamation
  • 31 July 1801 — Carnatic Treaty
  • 24 October 1801 — Marudhu Brothers executed
  • 16 November 1801 — Oomathurai and Sevathaiah executed
  • 31 July 1805 — Dheeran Chinnamalai executed
  • 10 July 1806 — Vellore Revolt
Leader–Place Associations
  • Puli Thevar — Nerkattumseval
  • Ondiveeran — Puli Thevar’s army
  • Velu Nachiyar — Sivaganga
  • Muthu Vaduganatha Thevar — Kalaiyar Kovil
  • Gopala Nayak — Virupachi and Dindigul League
  • Kattabomman — Panchalankurichi
  • Kattabomman’s execution — Kayathar
  • Sivasubramanianar’s execution — Nagalapuram
  • Marudhu Brothers — Sivaganga and Siruvayal
  • Marudhu Brothers’ execution — Tiruppattur
  • Oomathurai — Panchalankurichi
  • Dheeran Chinnamalai — Odanilai
  • Dheeran Chinnamalai’s execution — Sankagiri
  • Sepoy uprising — Vellore Fort
Leader–Ally Associations
  • Puli Thevar — western Palayakkarars and Travancore forces
  • Velu Nachiyar — Gopala Nayak, Hyder Ali and Marudhu Brothers
  • Gopala Nayak — Dindigul League
  • Kattabomman — Oomathurai and interest in the Marudhu confederacy
  • Marudhu Brothers — Gopala Nayak, Oomathurai, Kerala Varma and Mysore-associated leaders
  • Dheeran Chinnamalai — Tipu Sultan and French military training
  • Vellore sepoys — attempted restoration through Fateh Hyder
High-Yield Distinctions
Palayam versus Palayakkarar

Palayam

  • Territory
  • Military camp
  • Small domain

Palayakkarar

  • Holder or chief of the Palayam
  • Called Poligar by the British
Eastern versus Western Palayams

Eastern

  • Sattur
  • Nagalapuram
  • Ettayapuram
  • Panchalankurichi

Western

  • Uthumalai
  • Thalavankottai
  • Naduvakurichi
  • Singampatti
  • Seithur
Puli Thevar versus Kattabomman

Puli Thevar

  • Nerkattumseval
  • 1755–1767
  • Confederacy of western Palayakkarars
  • Battle of Kalakadu

Kattabomman

  • Panchalankurichi
  • Major confrontation in 1798–1799
  • Collector Jackson
  • Executed at Kayathar
Velu Nachiyar versus Marudhu Brothers

Velu Nachiyar

  • Displaced ruler of Sivaganga
  • Alliance with Hyder Ali and Gopala Nayak
  • Recovered Sivaganga in 1780

Marudhu Brothers

  • Commanders and administrators
  • Organised South Indian Confederacy
  • Issued the 1801 proclamation
Kattabomman Conflict versus South Indian Rebellion

Kattabomman conflict

  • Centred on Panchalankurichi
  • Main phase in 1799
  • Led by Kattabomman

South Indian Rebellion

  • Wider regional confederacy
  • 1800–1801
  • Led mainly by Marudhu Brothers
Oomathurai versus Kattabomman

Kattabomman

  • Executed in 1799

Oomathurai

  • Continued the resistance
  • Escaped prison in 1801
  • Rebuilt Panchalankurichi
  • Joined the Marudhu Brothers
Tiruchirappalli Proclamation versus Carnatic Treaty

Proclamation

  • Anti-British public appeal
  • June 1801
  • Issued by Marudhu Brothers

Carnatic Treaty

  • Expanded direct Company control
  • 31 July 1801
  • Ended the Palayakkarar political-military system
Palayakkarar Revolts versus Vellore Revolt

Palayakkarar Revolts

  • Led by regional chiefs
  • Defence of territorial authority
  • Forts, confederacies and guerrilla warfare

Vellore Revolt

  • Led by Indian sepoys
  • Military and religious grievances
  • Centred on Vellore Fort
  • Attempted restoration of Tipu Sultan’s family
Vellore 1806 versus Revolt of 1857

Vellore

  • Confined mainly to one fort
  • Suppressed within hours
  • No immediate widespread civilian rebellion

1857

  • Spread across major areas of northern and central India
  • Combined military and civilian rebellion
  • Lasted for several months
Exam Traps
  • Puli Thevar, not Kattabomman, led the earliest major Palayakkarar resistance covered in the Tamil Nadu textbook.
  • Ondiveeran served under Puli Thevar.
  • Velu Nachiyar took refuge with Gopala Nayak at Virupachi.
  • Gopala Nayak organised the Dindigul League.
  • Kattabomman met Jackson at Ramanathapuram on 19 September 1798.
  • The inquiry committee cleared Kattabomman and Jackson was dismissed.
  • Major Bannerman led the attack on Panchalankurichi.
  • Kattabomman was executed at Kayathar, not Panchalankurichi.
  • Sivasubramanianar was executed at Nagalapuram.
  • Oomathurai escaped from Palayamkottai prison and rebuilt Panchalankurichi.
  • The Marudhu rebellion is called the South Indian Rebellion or Second Palayakkarar War.
  • The 1801 proclamation was issued by the Marudhu Brothers.
  • The proclamation was displayed at Tiruchirappalli Fort and Srirangam.
  • The Carnatic Treaty was dated 31 July 1801.
  • Seventy-three rebels were transported to Penang.
  • Dheeran Chinnamalai was executed at Sankagiri.
  • Sir John Cradock introduced the military regulations connected with the Vellore Revolt.
  • Fateh Hyder was proclaimed ruler by the Vellore rebels.
  • Colonel Gillespie suppressed the Vellore Revolt.
  • Tipu Sultan’s family was transferred to Calcutta after the revolt.
  • Detailed women’s participation must be continued in Chapter 19 without duplicating this entire military chronology.
